title: Flux across a curve
objectives: Compute the flux of a field across a curve, and link it to divergence.

screens.title: What crosses the circle
screens.prose: Picture each field as a liquid flowing. The outward field $(x, y)$ and the rotation field $(-y, x)$ both have speed 1 on the unit circle. Flip between them.
screens.question: Which field carries liquid out of the circle?

options.why: Its arrows run along the circle, so nothing crosses it.
Same speed, different direction: only arrows that cross the circle carry liquid out.

options.text: Neither: a closed circle traps the flow
options.why: The outward arrows cross the circle at every point.

hints.text: Look at the angle between each field's arrows and the circle.
Outward arrows cross it at right angles.
Rotation arrows are tangent to it.

feedback.correct: Only the outward field crosses the circle.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which arrows cross the circle rather than run along it.

explain.text: Flow out of a curve counts the part of $\mathbf F$ across it, not along it. The rotation field is tangent to the circle, so its flux is 0.

screens.title: Flux across a curve
screens.prose: The **flux** across $C$ is $\oint_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf n\,ds$, with $\mathbf n$ the outward unit normal. On the unit circle $\mathbf n = (\cos t, \sin t)$ and $ds = dt$.
screens.question: What is the outward flux of $(x, y)$ across the unit circle?

hints.text: On the circle $\mathbf F = (\cos t, \sin t) = \mathbf n$.

feedback.correct: $\mathbf F \cdot \mathbf n = 1$ all round: flux $2\pi$. The rotation field gives 0.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Dot $\mathbf F$ with the normal, not the tangent.

byKey.zero: 0 is the work, or the rotation field's flux. The outward field crosses the circle.
byKey.pi: That is the area. The flux integrates over the length $2\pi$.

explain.text: $\mathbf F \cdot \mathbf n = \cos^2 t + \sin^2 t = 1$, so the flux is $2\pi$. For $(-y, x)$, $\mathbf F \cdot \mathbf n = 0$ and the flux is 0.

screens.title: Which normal points out
screens.prose: Take $C$ traversed counterclockwise, with step $d\mathbf r = (dx, dy)$. The four arrows, built from $dx$ and $dy$, are the candidates for $\mathbf n\,ds$ at one point.
screens.question: Which is the outward $\mathbf n\,ds$ for a counterclockwise curve?

options.why: That points inwards: the left side of a counterclockwise walk is the inside.
That is $d\mathbf r$, the tangent. Work uses it; flux uses the normal.
That is the tangent reversed, still along the curve.

hints.text: Turn it a quarter turn clockwise to point out.

feedback.correct: $\mathbf n\,ds = (dy, -dx)$, so $\mathbf F \cdot \mathbf n\,ds = P\,dy - Q\,dx$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Turn the tangent a quarter turn towards the outside.

explain.text: Counterclockwise, the inside is on the left, so outward is the tangent turned clockwise: $(dy, -dx)$. Hence flux $= \oint_C P\,dy - Q\,dx$.

screens.title: Green in normal form
screens.prose: We want $\oint_C P\,dy - Q\,dx$ as a double integral. Let $C$ be a piecewise smooth simple closed curve, counterclockwise round $D$. Green holds for any field with continuous partials on an open set containing $D$.
screens.question: Put the derivation in order.

lines.text: $\oint_C P\,dy - Q\,dx = \oint_C (-Q)\,dx + P\,dy$. (Rearrange: a work integral of the field $(-Q, P)$.)
The curl of $(-Q, P)$ is $\partial_x P - \partial_y(-Q) = P_x + Q_y$. (Definition of the curl.)
By Green, $\oint_C (-Q)\,dx + P\,dy = \iint_D (P_x + Q_y)\,dA$. (Green for $(-Q, P)$.)
The curl of $(-Q, P)$ is $Q_x - P_y$. (Same as for $\mathbf F$.)
lines.why: Rotating the field changes its curl: for $(-Q, P)$ it is $P_x + Q_y$.

hints.text: Read $P\,dy - Q\,dx$ as work of a new field.
Its curl is the divergence of $\mathbf F$.

feedback.correct: Outward flux equals the integral of the divergence.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each line needs the one before it.

byKey.d1: You kept $\mathbf F$'s curl. The new field $(-Q, P)$ has curl $P_x + Q_y$.
byKey.left-out: All four true lines are needed.

explain.text: Flux of $\mathbf F$ is work of $(-Q, P)$, whose curl is $P_x + Q_y$. Green then gives $\oint_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf n\,ds = \iint_D \nabla \cdot \mathbf F\,dA$.

screens.title: Out of a square
screens.prose: Take $(x, y)$ out of the unit square. Its divergence is 2 and the area is 1, so the normal form predicts 2. Check side by side: on each side, flux is the outward part of $\mathbf F$ times length.
screens.question: Fill in each side's outward flux and the total.

hints.text: On the right $\mathbf F \cdot \mathbf n = x = 1$.

feedback.correct: 1, 1, 0 and 0: total 2, as the divergence predicted.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Dot $\mathbf F$ with each side's outward normal.

byKey.work: 0 is the work round the square. Flux uses the normal, not the tangent.

explain.text: Right and top each give 1; left and bottom give 0. The total 2 is the divergence 2 times the area 1.

screens.title: A varying divergence
screens.prose: Take $\mathbf F = (x^2, y^2)$ out of the unit square. Now $\nabla \cdot \mathbf F = 2x + 2y$ varies.
screens.question: What is the outward flux?

hints.text: By sides: the right gives 1, the top 1, the others 0.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Integrate $2x + 2y$ over the square.

explain.text: $\iint (2x + 2y)\,dA = 2$. Directly, the right side has $P = 1$ and the top $Q = 1$, each over length 1; the other sides give 0.

screens.title: Out of a circle
screens.prose: Take $\mathbf F = (x^3, y^3)$ out of the unit circle. Its divergence is $3x^2 + 3y^2 = 3r^2$; use $dA = r\,dr\,d\theta$.
screens.question: What is the outward flux?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Integrate $3r^2$ with $dA = r\,dr\,d\theta$.

byKey.no-r: You used $dA = dr\,d\theta$: $\int_0^1 3r^2\,dr \times 2\pi = 2\pi$. Include the factor $r$.

screens.title: Normal, not tangent
screens.prose: Back to $(x, y)$ across the unit circle, counterclockwise. A learner writes $\oint_C P\,dx + Q\,dy$ for the flux.
screens.question: What is the outward flux, to 3 decimal places?

byKey.work: You used $P\,dx + Q\,dy$, the work. The outward field does no work round the circle but carries $2\pi$ across it.
byKey.inward: You used the inward normal $(-dy, dx)$, which flips the sign.

explain.text: $P\,dx + Q\,dy$ is the tangential part, which is 0 here. The normal part $P\,dy - Q\,dx$ is $1\,dt$, giving $2\pi \approx 6.283$. The inward normal would give $-2\pi$.

screens.title: The source field's hole
screens.prose: Lesson 5's source $\mathbf F = \tfrac{(x, y)}{x^2 + y^2}$ has divergence 0 off the origin. On a circle of radius $a$ about the origin, $\mathbf F \cdot \mathbf n = \tfrac1a$ and the length is $2\pi a$.
screens.question: Which circles carry flux $2\pi$?

options.text: Every circle that goes round the origin, whatever its radius
Every circle, including the one centred at $(3, 0)$
options.why: That circle and its inside miss the origin, where the divergence 0 really applies: its flux is 0.

options.text: None: the divergence is 0, so every flux is 0
options.why: The normal form needs $\mathbf F$ defined on the whole disc. Discs round the origin contain the hole.

hints.text: A disc that avoids the origin has divergence 0 throughout.

feedback.correct: Every circle round the origin carries $2\pi$; the one at $(3, 0)$ carries 0.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which discs contain the hole?

explain.text: Round the origin the flux is $\tfrac1a \cdot 2\pi a = 2\pi$ for every $a$. The normal form applies only to regions where $\mathbf F$ is smooth, so the hole carries the $2\pi$.

screens.title: A circle that misses the hole
screens.prose: The circle of radius 1 centred at $(3, 0)$ and its inside stay away from the origin.
screens.question: What is the source field's outward flux across this circle?

hints.text: Is $\mathbf F$ smooth on the whole disc?
Yes: the origin is outside it.

feedback.correct: 0: what flows in on the left flows out on the right.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Apply the normal form on this disc.

byKey.hole: $2\pi$ belongs to circles round the origin. This one misses it.

explain.text: The disc avoids the origin, so the normal form applies and gives $\iint 0\,dA = 0$. Liquid enters on the near side and leaves on the far side in equal amounts.

screens.title: Probability flowing in
screens.prose: A two-factor mean-reverting model drifts with $\boldsymbol\mu = (-0.5x, -0.5y)$. Think of a cloud of states, at density 1 near the circle just now, moving with the drift. Its flux across a curve is the rate probability crosses it.
screens.question: What is the outward flux of $\boldsymbol\mu$ across the unit circle, to 3 decimal places?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the divergence by the area.

byKey.pos: The sign matters: the drift points inwards, so the outward flux is negative.
byKey.half: You used one factor's $-0.5$. The divergence adds both: $-1$.

explain.text: $\nabla \cdot \boldsymbol\mu = -1$, so the flux is $-\pi$. Outflow equals the integral of the divergence: the same bookkeeping gives the heat and Fokker-Planck equations in the PDEs course.

screens.title: Reading the sign
screens.prose: The outward flux of the drift across the unit circle is $-\pi$.
screens.question: What does the negative sign say?

options.text: More probability enters the disc than leaves: states crowd towards the long-run level

options.why: Outward flux is negative, so the net flow is inwards.
Probability is conserved: it piles up near the centre.
Spin is curl, which is 0 here. The sign of flux is about crossing the curve.

hints.text: Outward flux counts out minus in.
Mean reversion pulls states to the centre.

feedback.correct: Net inflow: states crowd towards the long-run level.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Outward flux is out minus in.

explain.text: A negative outward flux is a net inflow. Probability is conserved, so its density inside rises: the cloud concentrates near the long-run level.

ideas: Flux across $C$ is $\oint_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf n\,ds = \oint_C P\,dy - Q\,dx$, with $\mathbf n\,ds = (dy, -dx)$ outward for counterclockwise $C$.
Let $D$ lie inside a piecewise smooth simple closed $C$. For $\mathbf F$ continuously differentiable on an open set containing $D$, the flux is $\iint_D \nabla \cdot \mathbf F\,dA$.
A hole where $\mathbf F$ is undefined can carry flux: the source gives $2\pi$ round the origin despite divergence 0.
summary.trap: Computing the work $\oint P\,dx + Q\,dy$ instead of the flux $\oint P\,dy - Q\,dx$.

quiz.prose: $\mathbf F = (2x, 3y)$ and $C$ is the circle of radius 2, counterclockwise.
quiz.question: What is the outward flux across $C$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the divergence by the area.

byKey.unit: $5\pi$ uses the unit disc. This disc has area $4\pi$.

explain.text: $\nabla \cdot \mathbf F = 2 + 3 = 5$, constant, and the disc's area is $4\pi$. The flux is $20\pi$.

quiz.question: What is the outward flux of $(-y, x)$ across any simple closed curve?

byKey.curl: 2 is the curl. Flux uses the divergence, $0 + 0$.

explain.text: $P_x + Q_y = 0 + 0$, so by the normal form of Green the flux is 0 across every simple closed curve.

quiz.question: For a counterclockwise $C$, which integral is the outward flux of $(P, Q)$?

options.why: That is the work, using the tangent.
That uses the inward normal: minus the flux.
That pairs each entry with its own direction, which is neither.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use the outward normal $(dy, -dx)$.

explain.text: Outward $\mathbf n\,ds = (dy, -dx)$, so $\mathbf F \cdot \mathbf n\,ds = P\,dy - Q\,dx$.

quiz.prose: The source $\tfrac{(x, y)}{x^2 + y^2}$, across the circle of radius 5 about the origin.
quiz.question: What is the outward flux?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. $\mathbf F \cdot \mathbf n = \tfrac15$ on this circle.

byKey.zero: The divergence is 0 off the origin, but this disc contains the hole.
byKey.ten: $10\pi$ is the length. Each piece carries $\tfrac15$.

explain.text: $\mathbf F \cdot \mathbf n = \tfrac15$ over a length $10\pi$, so the flux is $2\pi$, the same for every circle round the origin.
